Why “boring” and proven technologies are often the best choice for your project, and blindly following trends ends in a production disaster.
Every engineer goes through this phase. You buy a beautifully published new book, devour dozens of hours of IT conference talks on YouTube, and suddenly feel like you’ve had an epiphany. Design patterns, clean architecture, microservices powered by the magic of Domain-Driven Design… You wonder how it’s possible that you and your team have lived in such ignorance until now.
With a head full of ideals, you return to work on Monday and suddenly see that old, good-natured monolith through your new, “enlightened” eyes. You start to believe that this new, revolutionary technology or concept will solve all the problems in your system.
That is exactly what happened in my case. Unfortunately, I forgot one key rule: just because a tool is brilliant in the context of Netflix or Uber doesn’t mean it will work in a system where daily traffic resembles a local gas station rather than a massive highway.
Here is a story about how I fell into the trap of Hype Driven Development and why we paid the highest possible price for it in production.
Reality Check: When CRUD Becomes a Monster
The project was seemingly trivial. Our task was to create a new B2B order management module within an existing system. The business requirements essentially boiled down to accepting a form, validating a few fields, saving a record to a relational database, and sending an email notification. A classic, almost textbook CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete).
I could have written it in a few days. Instead… I remembered my recent reading.

I started convincing the team that this was the perfect moment to “do it right.” After all, this module would certainly grow! I used a programmer’s most powerful weapon: buzzwords. I threw around terms like scalability, loose coupling, and team autonomy.
As a result, we put a simple form through a meat grinder called Overengineering:

• Instead of a simple application, we extracted three separate microservices (one for validation, one for saving, and a third for notifications).

• We layered it with heavy abstractions inspired by DDD (using Aggregates where a simple database row would have sufficed).

• Instead of direct requests (REST/RPC), we introduced Event-Driven communication via a message broker.
We were proud. We had created an architectural masterpiece. The problem was that this masterpiece didn’t fit the framework we had to work within at all.
The Hidden Costs of Abstraction: Team Frustration and Delivery Drop
The first cracks appeared very quickly, hitting directly at what we now call Developer Experience (DX).
Suddenly, adding a new, simple field to the order form was no longer a one-hour task. It required changes in three repositories, updating the schemas of messages sent through the broker, and a coordinated deployment across multiple environments.
Our simple system became a maintenance nightmare:

• Testing Paralysis: End-to-end testing locally meant having to spin up several Docker containers, databases, and queues on your laptop. Half of the team’s time was spent solving local environment issues.

• Cognitive Overload: Developers (especially the less experienced ones) got lost in a maze of interfaces, factories, and facades implemented by force (“because that’s what the Gang of Four book said”). Instead of focusing on business logic, they wasted energy untangling the architecture.

• Performance Drop: Every simple request now had to travel over the network, through a message broker, and across multiple databases, drastically increasing response times.
We built a system ready for Black Friday traffic to handle the load of a standard Tuesday afternoon. We created exactly what top specialists warn against — a distributed monolith. We combined the disadvantages of distributed architecture with the tight coupling typical of legacy systems.

The Turning Point: Production Fire and Painful Debugging
The moment of truth came faster than we expected. Intermittent bugs reported by clients started appearing in production: “My order was placed, I got the email, but I don’t see it on the order list.”
In our old monolithic CRUD, locating such a bug would have taken fifteen minutes. You check the database, look at the logs of a single server, and you’re done. In our brave new distributed world, it was like looking for a needle in a haystack. During a blizzard.
We collided with the brutal reality of distributed systems: the problem of eventual consistency.
It turned out that under increased load (or temporary network hiccups), the service accepting orders sent an event to the queue and happily reported success to the client. The email microservice worked lightning-fast, sending the confirmation. However, the microservice responsible for the “read” side (the user’s view) lagged behind — it hadn’t processed the database message yet, or even lost the transaction in case of an error (lacking proper transaction compensation, known as the Saga pattern).
Instead of a single, solid ACID database transaction (where everything ends in total success or a rollback), we introduced chaos. Debugging required jumping between the logs of three different applications and correlating them using unique IDs, which… of course, we forgot to consistently pass along everywhere.
A Lesson in Humility: In Defense of “Boring” Technology
The outage and the weeks spent patching our architectural “empty shell” cured me of the desire to implement novelties just for the sake of using them.
I realized that system architecture is not the place to fulfill personal developer ambitions (that’s what side projects and hackathons are for). The goal of architecture and technology is to deliver business value at the lowest possible cost, in a way that is easy to understand and maintain.
Today, I am a huge advocate of so-called Boring Technology. I choose PostgreSQL over complex NoSQL databases until I have irrefutable proof that a relational database won’t cope. I start projects with a well-organized monolith (a Majestic Monolith), where I separate logic into modules, and I extract microservices only when dictated by distinct scaling requirements or the absolute need for autonomy by a separate development team.
I also understood another absolutely crucial thing: learning on a living organism requires anesthesia. If, as a team, we truly feel that a new technology (e.g., a new database, broker, or framework) will help us in the long run, we never introduce it right away in business-critical modules (the Core Domain). If we want to experiment with a new approach, we pick a small, secondary service — for example, a module for generating minor reports or an internal admin panel. If we make a mistake there due to a lack of experience, nobody loses money, and we gain invaluable know-how before stepping onto the main stage.

How Do I Make Decisions Today? (My Checklist)
Before I let myself get carried away by the next wave of hype for a new technology or complex architectural pattern, I ask myself and the team a few key questions. Treat this as my sanity checklist:

• What business problem does this solve? (Are we doing this because it’s trendy, or because it actually relieves a specific pain point in the current system?)

• Do we have the skills in the team? (Introducing Kafka to a team that has spent their whole lives working with RabbitMQ or direct REST APIs is asking for maintenance trouble).

• Where are we deploying this for the first time? (The golden rule: never test novelties on a module that makes money. We always start with a safe “sandbox,” i.e., a secondary, small service).

• What is the cost of reversing this decision? (Is it an easily reversible decision, or a hard commitment for years?)

• Can we achieve the same result using simpler methods? (Instead of a notification microservice, wouldn’t a simple Cron and asynchronous database jobs suffice?)
Maturity in software engineering is often the art of saying “no.” It’s the ability to defend the simplest possible solution in a world shouting from all sides about the need for complexity. Because ultimately, no one pays us for the prettiest architecture on the slides, but for a reliably working product.
Have you ever overcomplicated a project because you believed too much in a new technology? Where do you usually test novelties in your projects? Share your stories about “distributed monoliths” in the comments!
